overview:
In Jain studies and broader Indological scholarship, “page citations” refer to the practice of indicating the exact page or page range in a modern printed or digital edition from which a quotation, paraphrase, or data point has been taken. Page citations are a core tool of academic transparency: they allow readers to verify claims, check context, and assess whether an author has represented a source fairly. In standard humanities referencing, a full bibliographic entry (author, title, publisher, place, year) is paired with in-text or footnote citations that include page numbers—for example, “Jaini 1979, p. 84” or “Dundas 2002, pp. 115–117.”

Within Jainology, however, page citations sit inside a layered system of referencing. For primary Jain scriptures—such as the Śvetāmbara Āgamas, Digambara canonical texts, or philosophical treatises like the Tattvārthasūtra—scholarly convention is to cite the canonical divisions of the text (book, chapter, verse, sūtra, gāthā) rather than the page numbers of any one modern edition. This mirrors wider practice for ancient and religious literature, where canonically numbered parts are stable across editions, but page numbers vary from publisher to publisher. Thus, a verse from the Uttarādhyayana-sūtra would be cited by sūtra and verse number, and only secondarily—if at all—by page number in a specific translation.

Page citations become most important when dealing with secondary literature on Jainism: modern monographs, edited volumes, journal articles, and reference works. Here, the International School for Jain Studies and other academic bodies explicitly require page numbers for any quotation or paraphrase from such works, alongside full bibliographic details (author, title, publisher, place, year). This ensures that readers can locate the exact passage in the cited book or article, even if they are using a different edition or format. In footnotes and reference lists, page citations may appear as single pages (p. 37), ranges (pp. 37–39), or multiple non-contiguous pages (pp. 37, 52, 89).

In practice, a careful Jain studies article will distinguish clearly between canonical citations and page citations. When citing a primary text, the author will give the canonical location (e.g., Tattvārthasūtra 5.21) and then, if needed, add the page number of a particular edition in parentheses for ease of consultation. When citing a modern commentary or scholarly analysis, the author will rely on page citations alone, because these works do not have universally shared verse or sūtra numbering. This separation helps maintain the authority of the canonical structure while still honoring modern editorial work.

Page citations also play a role in comparative and historical work. When scholars trace how a particular Jain doctrine—such as anekāntavāda, karma theory, or sallekhanā—has been interpreted over time, they must show precisely where each interpretation appears in the secondary literature. Page citations allow them to map interpretive trajectories, identify shifts in emphasis, and highlight disagreements between authors. In manuscript studies, page citations may be supplemented by folio numbers, line numbers, or catalog identifiers, but in printed critical editions the page remains the basic unit of reference.

From a methodological standpoint, page citations are part of a broader ethics of citation in Jain studies. They support non-attachment to personal opinion by making it clear which ideas are grounded in texts and which are the author’s own interpretations. They also protect against misrepresentation: when a claim about Jain ethics, ritual, or history is backed by a precise page citation, readers can check whether the cited passage truly supports the claim. For students and youth, learning to use page citations correctly is a key step in moving from devotional reading to academically responsible engagement with Jain sources.

Finally, page citations must be handled with care when dealing with sensitive topics—such as fasting, sallekhanā, medical decisions, or family conflict. In such cases, scholars are expected not only to cite pages accurately but also to contextualize the passages, indicate interpretive debates, and recommend consultation with qualified human authorities. Page citations, then, are not merely technical details; they are part of a disciplined, transparent, and ethically aware approach to studying and teaching Jainism.

primary_sources.title: ISJS-Transactions Author Guidelines (Jainology Research Journal)
primary_sources.author: International School for Jain Studies Editorial Board
primary_sources.translation: “If we cite something from a secondary (general) book, we need to provide: Name of the Author, Name of the Book, Publisher, Place of Publication, Year of Publication, Page no/s. If we cite something from a primary source like Agamas or any other ancient book like Tattvarthasutra, Samayasara etc., we need to provide: Name of the text, Name/number of the chapter, Verse no/title of the subject.”
primary_sources.notes: This guideline, issued for a refereed research journal on Jainism, explicitly distinguishes between page citations for secondary literature and canonical citations for primary texts. It reflects a widely accepted academic convention in Jain studies: modern books and articles are cited with page numbers, while classical Jain scriptures are cited by chapter and verse or sūtra. The document situates page citations within a broader requirement for full bibliographic information and detailed research discussion.

primary_sources.title: General Academic Style Guides on Classical and Religious Works
primary_sources.author: Various (APA Style, Classical Studies referencing guides)
primary_sources.translation: Modern style manuals for classical and religious texts state that when directly quoting such works, scholars should use canonically numbered parts common across editions (e.g., books, chapters, verses, lines) instead of page numbers. Page numbers are reserved for modern secondary literature and, in special cases, for particular annotated editions.
primary_sources.notes: Although not Jain-specific, these style guides underpin Jainology’s practice of citing primary Jain scriptures by canonical divisions rather than page numbers. They help explain why page citations are central for secondary sources but secondary or optional for primary texts. Jain studies journals and monographs often adapt these general rules to the specific structure of Jain canonical and post-canonical literature.

misconceptions.myth: Page numbers are the main or only way to cite Jain scriptures.
misconceptions.reality: For primary Jain texts—such as Āgamas, Tattvārthasūtra, or Samayasāra—the academically preferred method is to cite canonical divisions (book, chapter, verse, sūtra, gāthā). Page numbers from a particular edition may be added for convenience, but they are not the primary reference, because pagination varies across publishers and translations.

misconceptions.myth: If a citation includes a page number, it must be referring to a primary canonical text.
misconceptions.reality: In Jain studies, page citations most often refer to secondary literature: modern monographs, commentaries, journal articles, and encyclopedias. When a citation includes only a page number and no verse or sūtra, it usually indicates that the author is referencing a scholarly discussion or interpretation, not the canonical text itself.

misconceptions.myth: Page citations are a minor technical detail that can be omitted without affecting the quality of research.
misconceptions.reality: Accurate page citations are essential for scholarly rigor and transparency. They allow readers to verify quotations, check context, and evaluate whether an author has represented sources fairly. In Jainology, journals and academic programs treat missing or incorrect page citations as a serious weakness in research writing.

misconceptions.myth: Using page citations for sensitive topics like fasting or sallekhanā is enough to justify any practical advice.
misconceptions.reality: Page citations show where a passage or interpretation comes from, but they do not replace the need for careful contextualization, awareness of interpretive debates, and consultation with qualified human authorities. Especially for issues involving health, ethics, or family responsibilities, page citations must be paired with responsible guidance and explicit recognition of the limits of textual evidence.
